text.p: Gabon held the second round of its parliamentary elections on Sunday with 65 of the national assembly's 120 seats still to be decided but President Omar Bongo's ruling party on course for an outright majority.
Voting began slowly for the one seat still to be decided in the capital Libreville following the December 15 first round, witnesses said.
There was no immediate word on voting elsewhere although security forces were reinforced in Koulamoutou in the south following friction between rival supporters.
The elections are part of a democratic timetable brokered in Paris in 1994 after political violence shook the oil-producing Central African nation, killing more than a dozen people.
Bongo's Democratic Party won 47 of the 55 national assembly seats decided on December 15 and electoral officials say Bongo supporters took a lead into the run-offs for many of the undecided seats.
The main opposition National Woodcutters Rally (RNB), which won control of Libreville during chaotic October municipal elections, only managed three seats on December 15.
It and other opposition parties have called for the parliamentary elections to be rerun, denouncing problems with voter cards and electoral lists during the first round.
The elections are Gabon's second multiparty legislative polls. The first were in 1990 when a wave of democratic reform swept across Africa after the fall of Soviet-bloc communism.
Bongo has ruled the former French colony since 1968 after the death of Gabon's founding head of state, Leon Mba.
